'''Alicia Esther Nash''' ({{nee|'''Lardé Lopez-Harrison'''}}{{Family name footnote|Lardé|Lopez-Harrison|lang=Spanish}}; January 1, 1933 – May 23, 2015) was a Salvadoran-American physicist. The wife of mathematician [[John Forbes Nash Jr.]], she was a mental-health care advocate, who gave up her professional aspirations to support her husband and son, who were both diagnosed with [[schizophrenia]].

Her life with Nash was chronicled in the 1998 book, [[A Beautiful Mind (book)|''A Beautiful Mind'']] by [[Sylvia Nasar]], as well as in the 2001 film [[A Beautiful Mind|of the same title]] directed by [[Ron Howard]], in which she was portrayed by [[Jennifer Connelly]].<ref name=rebellious>[https://www.thestar.com/news/insight/2015/05/29/alicia-nashs-beautiful-complex-rebellious-life.html "Alicia Nash’s beautiful, complex, rebellious life"], ''Toronto Star'', May 29, 2015. Retrieved May 30, 2015.</ref><ref name="nj.com">[http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2015/05/funeral_for_john_nash_and_wife_to_be_private_alumn.html "Funeral for John Nash and wife to be private; Alumni group plans memorial"], ''The Star-Ledger'', May 26, 2015. Retrieved May 27, 2015.</ref>

== Personal life ==
Alicia Lardé Lopez-Harrison was born on January 1, 1933, in El Salvador, the daughter of Alicia Lopez-Harrison and Carlos Lardé, a doctor. The Lardé Lopez-Harrison family also included two boys, Carlos and Rolando Lardé. Both of her parents came from socially prominent, well-travelled families who spoke several languages. Her aunt was the poet [[Alice Lardé de Venturino]]; her paternal grandfather was Jorge Lardé, a chemical engineer.<ref>[https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/amex/nash/peopleevents/p_anash.html Alicia Nash biography] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170302182348/https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/amex/nash/peopleevents/p_anash.html |date=March 2, 2017 }}. Retrieved May 27, 2015</ref>

When Lardé was a child, her father traveled to the United States a few times before deciding to move the family there permanently in 1944. After first settling in [[Biloxi, Mississippi]], the family later moved to New York City.<ref name="VásquezGuerrero" >{{cite news|last1=Vásquez|first1=Verónica|last2=Guerrero|first2=Francisca|title=Alicia Lardé de Nash: Refugio de un Genio|url=https://issuu.com/lpglaprensagrafica/docs/31817|accessdate=September 19, 2017|newspaper=[[La Prensa Gráfica]]|date=March 22, 2002|location=Antiguo Cuscatlan, El Salvador|pages=118–119|language=Spanish|trans-title=Alicia Lardé Nash: Refuge of a genius|archive-date=September 19, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170919185736/https://issuu.com/lpglaprensagrafica/docs/31817|url-status=dead}}</ref> Lardé was accepted to the [[Marymount School of New York|Marymount School]] with the help of a letter of recommendation from El Salvador's Ambassador to the United States.{{who|date=May 2015}} Following graduation from Marymount,{{citation needed|date=May 2015}} Lardé was accepted into [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], to study physics. She was one of very few women studying at MIT in the 1950s. There she met her future husband, [[John Forbes Nash, Jr.]]<ref name="VásquezGuerrero" />

Despite signs of Nash's mental illness which had emerged in the early 1950s,<ref name="NYReview of Books" /><ref name="NYTimes News Service" >[http://www.u.arizona.edu/~mwalker/NashStory.htm The Lost Years of a Nobel Laureate] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605045913/http://www.u.arizona.edu/~mwalker/NashStory.htm |date=June 5, 2011 }}. Retrieved May 27, 2015</ref> the couple married in 1957. In 1958, Alicia became pregnant with their son, John Charles Martin Nash.<ref name="NYTimes News Service" /> Like his father, John Charles would later develop schizophrenia.<ref name="VásquezGuerrero" /> Shortly before their son's birth in 1959, Nash was [[involuntary commitment|committed]] to [[McLean Hospital]] to receive psychiatric treatment for his illness.<ref name="NYTimes News Service" /> After spending 50 days in hospital, he was released,<ref name="VásquezGuerrero" /> but over the following years he was [[involuntary commitment|committed]] three more times, including commitments initiated by his sister.<ref name="NYReview of Books" /> The strain of his illness led to the couple's divorce in 1963. After Nash's mother died in 1968, he asked Alicia to allow him to return to live with her. He moved back in with her in 1970, and although they remained divorced, Alicia cared for her former husband for many years. The couple remarried in 2001.<ref name="VásquezGuerrero" />

In 2002, the couple visited her native country, El Salvador, where she was honored by President [[Francisco Flores Pérez]] with a tribute to her life.<ref name="Fallecen la salvadoreña Alicia Lardé y nobel de economía John Nash en accidente" >[https://www.laprensagrafica.com/internacional/Fallecen-la-salvadorena-Alicia-Larde-y-nobel-de-economia-John-Nash-en-accidente-20150524-0032.html La Prensa Grafica]. Retrieved March 18, 2019</ref>

== Career ==
After graduation from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], Nash went to work for the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory|Brookhaven Nuclear Development Corporation]] as a lab physicist.{{citation needed|date=May 2015}} In the early 1960s, she worked for [[RCA Corporation|RCA]] as an aerospace engineer, but was laid off. She then worked for years at [[Con Edison]] as a system programmer and later for the [[New Jersey Transit]] system as a [[Programmer|computer programmer]] and [[Data analysis|data analyst]].<ref name="VásquezGuerrero" /><ref name="NYReview of Books">{{cite magazine|last1=Didion|first1=Joan|title=Varieties of Madness|url=http://www.nybooks.com/articles/1998/04/23/varieties-of-madness/|accessdate=September 20, 2017|magazine=[[The New York Review of Books]]|date=April 23, 1998|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170813223357/http://www.nybooks.com/articles/1998/04/23/varieties-of-madness/|archivedate=August 13, 2017|location=New York City}}</ref> She was a member of numerous women's engineering societies.{{citation needed|date=May 2015}} When the film ''A Beautiful Mind'' was released, Alicia Nash was serving as president of MIT's Alumni Association Board.<ref>[http://www.nj.com/healthfit/index.ssf/2015/05/alicia_nash_was_loyal_heart_to_john_nashs_beautifu.html Alicia Nash was loyal heart]. Retrieved May 28, 2015</ref>

== Mental health advocacy ==
Nash became a spokesperson for schizophrenia and mental illness.{{when|date=May 2015}} In 2005 she was given the Luminary Award from the [[Brain & Behavior Research Foundation]]. She travelled around the country to discuss rights for those with mental illness, and in 2009 she met with New Jersey state lawmakers to discuss how to improve that state's mental health care system. In 2012, she was honored at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]'s John and Alicia Nash Conference for her support of those with mental illness, where she delivered the keynote address.<ref>[http://www.mhatexas.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/August-2012-Final.pdf UTA Symposium] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150529113247/http://www.mhatexas.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/August-2012-Final.pdf |date=May 29, 2015 }} accessed May 29, 2015</ref><ref>[http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/03/a_beautiful_challenge_to_help.html John Nash and family advocate for mental health care]. Retrieved May 28, 2015</ref><ref>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/alicia-nash-wife-of-nobel-laureate-dies-at-82/2015/05/27/6fced406-0479-11e5-bc72-f3e16bf50bb6_story.html Alicia Nash dies at 82]. Retrieved May 28, 2015</ref>

== Death ==
{{Further|John Forbes Nash Jr.#Death}}
Alicia and her husband were killed in a car crash on the [[New Jersey Turnpike]] on May 23, 2015, in [[Monroe Township, Middlesex County, New Jersey|Monroe Township]], [[New Jersey]]. They were on their way home after a visit to Norway, where her husband had been awarded the [[Abel Prize]]. The driver of the [[taxicab]] they were riding in from [[Newark Liberty International Airport|Newark Airport]] lost control of the cab and struck a guardrail. Because neither were wearing seatbelts, both passengers were ejected and killed.<ref>{{cite news|title=Famed 'A Beautiful Mind' mathematician John Nash, wife, killed in N.J. Turnpike crash|last=Ma|first=Myles|work=The Star-Ledger|url=http://www.nj.com/middlesex/index.ssf/2015/05/famed_a_beautiful_mind_mathematician_wife_killed_in_taxi_crash_police_say.html|date=May 23, 2015|accessdate=May 23, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title='A Beautiful Mind' mathematician John Nash, wife killed in crash|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2015/05/24/john-nash-dies/27879515/|accessdate=May 24, 2015|agency=USA News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title='Beautiful Mind' mathematician John Nash killed in crash|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-32865248|accessdate=May 24, 2015|work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Princeton mathematician John Nash and his wife, Alicia, are killed in a car accident|url=http://qz.com/411383/princeton-mathematician-john-nash-and-his-wife-alicia-are-killed-in-a-car-accident/|accessdate=May 24, 2015|agency=Quartz}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=John Nash, mathematician who inspired 'A Beautiful Mind', killed in car crash|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-people-nash-idUSKBN0O90JR20150524|work=Reuters|date=May 24, 2015 |accessdate=May 24, 2015}}</ref>

== Portrayal in media ==
Alicia was portrayed by [[Jennifer Connelly]] in the 2001 film ''[[A Beautiful Mind]]''. For her performance, Connelly won the [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress]], mentioning Nash during her acceptance speech.<ref name="nj.com" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://aaspeechesdb.oscars.org/results.aspx?AC=PREV_RECORD&XC=/results.aspx&BU=http%3A%2F%2Faaspeechesdb.oscars.org%2F&TN=aatrans&SN=AUTO6920&SE=1616&RN=1&MR=0&TR=0&TX=1000&ES=0&CS=0&XP=&RF=WebReportList&EF=&DF=WebReportOscars&RL=0&EL=0&DL=0&NP=255&ID=&MF=oscarsmsg.ini&MQ=&TI=0&DT=&ST=0&IR=0&NR=0&NB=0&SV=0&SS=0&BG=&FG=&QS=&OEX=ISO-8859-1&OEH=utf-8 |title=Academy Awards database |website=aaspeechesdb.oscars.org |access-date=May 30, 2015}}</ref> Writing in the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', Lisa Navarrette criticized Connelly's casting as an example of [[Whitewashing in film|whitewashing]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Navarrette |first1=Lisa |title=Why the Whitewashing of Alicia Nash? |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2002-apr-01-et-navarrete1-story.html |access-date=January 6, 2021 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 1, 2002}}</ref>
